items.question: What is the difference between a CloudWatch metric and a CloudWatch alarm?
options: A metric is the raw number; an alarm is the rule + notification when a threshold is crossed
An alarm is the raw number; a metric is only the email template
They are the same thing with two names
Metrics only exist in Billing, alarms only exist in IAM
items.ren_hint_english: Metric = data. Alarm = decision on that data.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Metric = number. Alarm = threshold cross aana notify.
items.explanation: CloudWatch collects metrics automatically. You set alarms so problems find you — not the other way around.

items.question: Why set a CPU alarm to fire after 5 consecutive minutes above 90%, not on the first 1-second spike?
options: Evaluation period filters noise — sustained problems matter more than momentary spikes
AWS forbids any alarm under 5 minutes always
Metrics are only collected once per day
Alarms cannot send email unless you wait 5 minutes
items.ren_hint_english: Short spikes are normal; sustained high CPU is the real signal.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Momentary spike normal — 5 minutes sustained = real problem.
items.explanation: Evaluation periods reduce false alarms so you only wake up for issues that need action.

items.question: Why is 'we'll check the dashboard occasionally' a weak monitoring strategy?
options: Dashboards need a human looking; alarms notify you even at 3am
Dashboards are illegal in AWS
CloudWatch cannot show CPU metrics
Budgets replace the need for any monitoring
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Dashboard paakura alavukku mattum illa — alarm unna thedum.
items.explanation: Problems do not wait for office hours. Alarms reach you; dashboards give context after.

items.situation: Production is down. CloudWatch shows: EC2 CPU 12% (very low), ALB request count near zero, RDS CPU 98% (very high).
items.question: What is the most likely root cause?
options: The database is overloaded — app/EC2 are idle waiting; traffic fails or times out
EC2 is out of CPU and needs a bigger instance immediately
S3 Block Public Access caused the outage
The Region selector was set to the wrong city
items.ren_hint_english: Low EC2 + high RDS + zero traffic → look at the database first.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: EC2 low, RDS 98%, traffic zero — database thaan problem.
items.explanation: Pattern reading: RDS is saturated, EC2 waits, ALB sees unhealthy/failed paths. Fix the DB bottleneck.

items.situation: A test environment was left running for 6 weeks. Month-end bill: ₹4.2 lakhs. No budget alert existed.
items.question: What should have been set up before anything went live?
options: An AWS Budget with alerts (e.g. 80% / 100%) plus a cleanup habit for test resources
Nothing — billing surprises are normal and unavoidable
Only CloudWatch dashboards with no alarms and no budgets
Sharing the root password so anyone can check cost manually
items.ren_hint_english: Budget alerts catch burn early; tagging/cleanup prevents idle waste.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Budget alert + test resource cleanup habit — invoice shock avoid aagum.
items.explanation: Set cost budgets before spend. Also tag and expire test environments so idle NAT/EC2/EBS cannot run for weeks unnoticed.

items.situation: Before going live, Day 5 taught a minimum safety set: watch the system and watch the spend.
items.question: Name the AWS service used for metrics and alarms. (Type the service name)
items.ren_hint_english: Monitoring service that receives metrics from EC2, S3, RDS, and more.
items.explanation: CloudWatch = system health. Billing / Budgets / Cost Explorer = spend health. You need both.
